https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg9.text: Image source, Instagram: sydney_marathon Image caption, The medal design appears to show Munich's Allianz Arena on the bottom-right By Harry Sekulich Reporting from Sydney Published 4 hours ago One week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers face questions about whether designers etched the wrong city's stadium on the participation medal. The medal appears to feature a stadium carved in the likeness of Allianz Arena in the German city of Munich, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney â which the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course runs past. The BBC has reached out to Sydney Marathon for comment. Some 40,000 runners will be taking part in the event on 30 August, after more than 120,000 ballot entries. Speculation about a possible mix-up began after Sydney Marathon's official social media account unveiled its design for the 2026 medal, inviting users to "look closely and you'll find the story of the course in the details". They continued: "A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way - starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Munich arena (bottom) appears to feature on the medal instead of the Sydney landmark Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly-named Allianz Stadium has a flatter faÃ§ade smoothed with long bronze fins. The other face of the double-sided medal features a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian. Forty-two half-round markings lining the circular edge "represent each kilometre of the course", organisers explained. Killian told the BBC he was not responsible for the other artwork. Image source, Instagram: sydney_marathon Image caption, The front of the Sydney Marathon medal features an artwork by Ambrose Killian The blunder follows a similar incident at last year's Great North Run in Newcastle, where medals mistakenly featured the Sunderland and Wear River â which is not part of the event. Sydney was announced as the seventh city added to the Abbott majors series in 2024, joining London, Berlin, Boston, Chicago, New York, and Tokyo. Cape Town is set to become the eighth city when it hosts its first marathon major next year. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Southport attack Southport attack families’ fury after 13 survivors miss out on school funding Six schools attended by girls injured in mass stabbing miss out on £1m allocated for staff, counselling and specialist support Josh Halliday North of England editor Tue 24 Nov 2026 11.37 EST Last modified on Tue 24 Nov 2026 11.52 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Families of girls injured in the Southport attack have said they are “horrified” that their daughters’ schools received no financial support after the atrocity while others were given “eye-watering sums”. It emerged on Tuesday that seven schools attended by victims of the mass stabbing received £1m between them to pay for extra teaching staff, counselling and other specialist support. However, six schools attended by 13 of the surviving girls were given no additional funding despite their pupils being “utterly traumatised”. Sefton council, which disclosed the figures, said it only offered support to schools that requested it, rather than approaching each one individually. The mother of a then-seven-year-old girl, who nearly died after being stabbed 33 times, said she was “horrified by the amount of money that has been given to some schools while we have had to fight for every penny to support our daughter”. She said they had fought a “private, anonymous, invisible battle to get our daughter the most basic support and care she needs at school”, and that this had eventually been provided by other councils. The mother, whose daughter cannot be identified by the media, said Sefton council should not have “put the responsibility on [headteachers] to ask for money” and that it should have contacted schools proactively. She added: “Sefton council has often used the phrase that it has supported the ‘most affected’ children, but our daughter went back to school with visible injuries. “Her classmates suffered trauma because they could see what had happened to her, yet they and her teachers received no funding for wellbeing support.” A mother of two sisters, then aged eight and 10, who survived the attack at a Taylor Swift holiday club, said Sefton council should be “ashamed” of its handling of the funds, which were part of a recovery grant from the government. “I feel absolutely disgusted by the huge discrepancies in the money that has been given to schools,” she said. “The council never spoke to us or asked us what we needed, meanwhile our daughters have been passed from pillar to post, moving schools to try and get the help they needed in class after everything they had been through.” The father of the two girls, who also cannot be named, added: “Nobody is suggesting schools shouldn’t have received funding. Nor should anyone question the importance of remembering the children whose lives were lost. “But what about those who survived; the children who were physically injured; those who witnessed the unimaginable; those who are still struggling with their education, their mental health and everyday life.” Nicola Ryan-Donnelly, partner at the Southport law firm Fletchers Solicitors, which represents many of the surviving girls’ families, described the funding disparity as “shameful and outrageous”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Average of 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion She said “eye-watering sums” had been handed out to single schools while others received nothing despite looking after girls “utterly traumatised by what they had witnessed and endured”. Sefton council said the school grants were part of a wider support package, and that it had never turned away a school that asked for help. It is understood that the council is willing to meet affected families to learn any lessons. A council spokesperson said: “The children, families and school communities affected by the events of July 2024 remain at the heart of Southport’s recovery and support of course continues. “Immediately following the 29th and 30th of July 2024, Sefton council had to make a series of decisions to provide urgent humanitarian assistance to the community of Southport. “This included making support available across Southport schools with additional funding available for schools facing specific pressures arising from the events. “Those pressures varied, as did the staffing, specialist support and other resources already available within each school who approached the council for help.” Explore more on these topics Southport attack School funding Schools England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students
